setting: A short lecture in an introductory biology class about how leaf cells capture light energy.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Today I want to focus on what happens inside a leaf when sunlight hits it.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert light energy into chemical energy stored as sugar.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Most of the work takes place in chloroplasts—tiny green structures packed with chlorophyll.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue and red wavelengths; green light is mostly reflected, which is why leaves look green to us.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In the first stage, called the light-dependent reactions, water molecules are split and oxygen is released as a by-product.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: That stage also produces energy carriers—ATP and NADPH—that power the next stage.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide from the air is fixed into sugar using those energy carriers.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Notice the plant does not “eat” sunlight the way animals eat food; it transforms light into a usable chemical form.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: If a plant gets too little light, sugar production slows, and growth can stall even when water and soil nutrients are available.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next class we'll look at how temperature and carbon dioxide levels change the rate of the Calvin cycle.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How leaf cells convert light into chemical energy
How to grow plants without any water
How animals digest sugar from plants

questions.explanation: The professor explains photosynthesis inside leaf cells: chloroplasts, light reactions, and the Calvin cycle.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—animals eating plants are not discussed; the focus is the plant’s energy conversion.
questions.correctAnswer: How leaf cells convert light into chemical energy

questions.narrator_text: According to the professor, why do leaves usually look green?

options.text: They absorb only green light for sugar production
They store green oxygen inside the stem
They paint the leaf surface with green minerals from soil
They reflect most green light while absorbing blue and red wavelengths

questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue and red light; green is mostly reflected, so leaves look green.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—green is reflected, not the main wavelength absorbed for the process described.
questions.correctAnswer: They reflect most green light while absorbing blue and red wavelengths

questions.narrator_text: What is released when water is split in the light-dependent reactions?
questions.explanation: She says water molecules are split and oxygen is released as a by-product.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A or D—those are not named as products of splitting water here.

questions.narrator_text: What can be inferred if a healthy plant receives very little light?

options.text: Chloroplasts will start absorbing only green light
It will immediately stop needing carbon dioxide forever
Sugar production may slow and growth can stall even with water and nutrients
The Calvin cycle will run faster than usual

questions.explanation: She notes that with too little light, sugar production slows and growth can stall even when water and nutrients are available.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing D—less light would not make the Calvin cycle faster in this talk.
questions.correctAnswer: Sugar production may slow and growth can stall even with water and nutrients
